chunks: What an ISR is. The question: What is an interrupt service routine (ISR)?
An ISR (interrupt service routine) is a function that the hardware runs for you when an interrupt happens.
It lets the CPU react at once to an event, such as a received byte, and then go straight back to its work. You never call it yourself, so it takes no inputs and returns nothing.
It passes results to the main code through shared variables.
You are reading a book when the phone rings. You use a bookmark, answer, write the message on a sticky note, hang up, and carry on. Later you read the sticky note.
The ISR is the quick call, and the sticky note is the shared variable. You do not choose when the phone rings. A long chat would make every other caller wait.
The ISR and main code never call each other; they exchange information through shared state. One side writes, the other reads.
That pattern, with exactly one writer per variable, keeps the shared-data problem manageable.
Interrupt: ("What interrupts are"): a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause and run a handler.
Vector table: ("How interrupts work and are implemented"): a list in memory holding the handler's address for each interrupt.
Flag: a bit in the peripheral (the hardware block, here the serial port) that says "I need service". The ISR must clear it, or the interrupt fires again at once.
volatile: a C keyword telling the compiler a variable can change behind its back, such as inside an ISR.
A UART (a serial port) receives a byte and sets a flag. The CPU pauses the main code and looks up the ISR's address in the vector table.
The ISR reads the byte, which also clears the flag, stores it in a buffer, and sets byte arrived to 1. Later the main code sees byte arrived and processes the byte.
At 115,200 bits per second a byte arrives about every 87 microseconds, so a 2 microseconds ISR uses only about 2. 3% of the CPU's time. That is the whole idea.

"An ISR is the function that the hardware calls when an interrupt happens: its address is in the vector table, it takes no arguments and returns nothing, and it interrupts the main code asynchronously.
A good one identifies the source, clears the flag, does the minimum work, like storing a received byte, and signals the main code through a volatile flag or buffer.
It must be short, can't block, and any data it shares with main must be volatile and accessed safely."
